opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'll be honest: management is not really my strength, and I've known that for a long time. When I created FAIR back in 2013, I had to do it, because somebody had to set up the lab, recruit people, define the culture, and convince the company that open research was the right way to go. I think I did a reasonable job at the founding part, the vision, attracting talent, and establishing the principle that we publish and open-source what we do.

But the day-to-day management, the budgets, the performance reviews, the organizational stuff, I'm not particularly good at it and I don't particularly enjoy it. So after a few years I stepped away from running the lab and took the role of chief scientist. Other people who are much better at it than I am took over the management side, and that turned out to be a much better arrangement for everybody.

What I think I'm good at is having a long-term scientific vision, identifying which directions are promising and which are dead ends, and mentoring people. I like working with students and young researchers and pointing them toward interesting problems. I also spend a lot of time on public advocacy, explaining what AI can and cannot do and arguing for open research and open-source platforms.

So for me, the ideal is a situation where I can influence the scientific direction and the culture without being bogged down in administration. A good research organization needs both: people with vision and people who can make the organization run. It's very rare to find both in the same person, and I'm certainly not one of those rare people.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he had to handle management when founding FAIR to set up the lab, then stepped away after a few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, management was never the thing I was drawn to. I became a scientist because I like to think about problems, build things, understand how they work. When I took on the role of leading FAIR, it was with the condition that I could keep doing research myself, and I did.

But I think my view of management is a bit unusual compared to a classical corporate view. When you run a research lab, you are not managing people in the sense of telling them what to do. If you have to tell a good researcher what to work on, you have hired the wrong person, or you have the wrong organization. The job is to hire people who are smarter than you in their domain, give them freedom, protect them from the pressures of the rest of the company, and set a direction, a kind of ambition, that people can rally around. In our case, that ambition was to understand intelligence and build machines that are intelligent. That is what attracts people.

So the strengths I could bring were not really about process or organization. They were about having a scientific vision, having good taste in which problems matter, and being willing to defend open research against short-term thinking. I spent a lot of time convincing people inside the company that publishing openly was good for the company, not just for science. That is a form of management, but it is really more like advocacy.

The parts I was bad at, the budgets, the performance reviews, the organizational politics, I tried to delegate to people who were good at them. And after a few years, I stepped back from running the lab day to day and became chief scientist, which fits me much better. I can influence the research direction, mentor people, say what I think is wrong with the current fashion, and spend my time on the ideas I actually care about. That is where I am most useful.

r001.rationale: The response says LeCun took on leading FAIR while continuing research and later stepped back, but it does not say he accepted management temporarily to get the organization started.

astra-6.text: I think my strengths are more in scientific direction than in day-to-day management. I like thinking about which problems we should work on, which approaches might work, and discussing ideas with researchers. That’s different from running an organization—making sure everything is coordinated, following up on people, dealing with all the operational details. Those are important skills, but they’re not what I most enjoy. So I think the right arrangement is to work with people who are good at those things and have complementary strengths.

r001.rationale: The response says he prefers scientific direction and working with people who handle operations, but does not say he was willing to manage temporarily to get the organization started.

sol-6.1.text: I think my strength is more in setting a research direction and working with people on ideas than in day-to-day management. Those are different skills. You can have a strong intuition about which scientific problems matter without being the best person to manage an organization. So I like working with people who complement me—who can handle the organizational side while I focus on the science.

r001.rationale: The response describes preferring to focus on science while others handle organizational work; it does not say LeCun would manage temporarily to get the organization started.
